source: Wang et al. (2026) PreFlect: from retrospective to prospective reflection in LLM agents, Tables 1 and 4 re-read (gap 7)
finding: Resolves the cross-checker's open point. The 58.18 total is the GPT-4.1 backbone. Plain Smolagents with GPT-4.1 scores 46.06. The 49.70 figure is HF-ODR with o1 in the leaderboard figure, not a Reflexion row. The Table 1 text layout is scrambled, so Reflexion and Self-Refine GAIA totals for GPT-4.1 were not read cleanly. In the ablation, removing the distilled planning-error prior costs more than removing re-planning.
numbers: GAIA validation, GPT-4.1, pass@1: Smolagents 46.06 (L1 56.60, L2 47.67, L3 19.23); with PreFlect 58.18 (71.70, 55.81, 38.46), +12.12 points. w/o planning errors (PE) 50.30; w/o dynamic re-planning (DRP) 51.52. So the error prior is worth 7.88 points and re-planning 6.66. Without the prior PreFlect is only +4.24 over baseline. Cost $46.31 to $54.48 (+17.64%). Defect rate: 74.44% of updated plans flagged risky, over 165 tasks. Transfer: OWL 50.30 to 60.61. Gemini-2.5-pro total 59.39.
limits: About 165 tasks, so one task is about 0.6 points. Single run, no seeds. Priors were distilled from 300 trajectories of the same agent on HotpotQA and MuSiQue, so this is stored lessons plus a prospective check, not a pure imagined premortem. With 74% of plans flagged risky, the check nearly always fires.
agent_relevance: Stored failure lessons carry most of the gain of a prospective check; imagined failure without the prior gave about +4 points. Supports pairing a premortem step with a small error memory (gap 7 partly closed) and warns that the check flags almost every plan (gap 3).

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing (ICLR 2024)
finding: Critique grounded in tools (search, code interpreter) improves answers. The same critique loop without tools gives little or negative change. The authors say the model's own critiques add only marginally, and self-correction can even worsen the initial answer.
numbers: ChatGPT, 500 questions each, F1: AmbigNQ CoT 64.3, CRITIC 74.9, CRITIC w/o tool 67.3. HotpotQA CoT 42.8, CRITIC 52.9, w/o tool 46.1. TriviaQA CoT 79.2, CRITIC 81.7, w/o tool 79.9. Text-davinci-003: AmbigNQ CoT 58.6, CRITIC 64.9, w/o tool 58.3; HotpotQA 46.1, 50.5, 46.1. Math: ChatGPT GSM8k PoT 72.5, CRITIC 78.2, w/o tool 77.0 (the no-tool loop kept most of the gain here). Text-davinci-003 GSM8k PoT 70.1, w/o tool 68.3 (-1.8); SVAMP 84.0 to 80.7 (-3.3) both with and without tool.
limits: Tool critique is not a premortem. It checks the answer rather than imagining failure. Search results were cached, greedy decoding, up to 3 correction rounds. Mixed on math: no-tool critique helped ChatGPT on GSM8k.
agent_relevance: Direct support for gap 4. On QA, tool-backed critique gave +6 to +10 F1; the internal-only loop gave 0 to +3. Tie any failure check to an external verifier where one exists.

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han, Zhang (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey
finding: Survey of self-correction papers. Finds no prior work showing successful self-correction from prompted-LLM feedback on general tasks, except tasks exceptionally suited to it. Self-correction works well when reliable external feedback exists. Large-scale fine-tuning also enables it. Many papers over-evaluate by using oracle information or weak initial prompts.
numbers: No table numbers; three headline findings read from abstract and introduction, plus the oracle-use discussion.
limits: Survey; the judgement is the authors' reading of the literature. Not a premortem study.
agent_relevance: Confirms the gating logic: a failure-imagining step with no external signal is the weakest form of self-critique. Keep it tied to a tool, test or retrieval result (gap 4).

source: Huang et al. (2024) LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning yet, Tables 2 and 3 re-read
finding: With oracle labels deciding when to stop, self-correction gains a lot. Without labels (intrinsic), accuracy drops on all benchmarks. Table columns are numbers of model calls (1, 3, 5), as the cross-checker noted. Models change correct answers to wrong ones more often than the reverse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic: GSM8K 75.9, 75.1, 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8, 38.1, 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0, 25.0, 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5, 91.5, 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0, 79.5, 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0, 49.0, 43.0. Oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5; HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0 (GPT-4 59.0). GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: The prompt asks the model to review its answer, not to imagine failure in advance. Reasoning and QA only; no tools.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 4: this is the downside a premortem step must avoid. The same paper shows self-consistency beats multi-agent debate at equal call count.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning in language models (ICLR 2023)
finding: Sampling many independent reasoning paths and taking the majority answer beats one greedy pass by large margins. This is the clearest pooled-samples-beat-one-pass result, but it pools answers, not failure lists.
numbers: PaLM-540B, 40 samples averaged over 10 runs: GSM8K 56.5 to 74.4 (+17.9), SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9.
limits: Pools answers, not failure causes. 40 samples is 40 times the cost of one pass. No one has tested pooling several independent premortem lists (gap 9 stays open).
agent_relevance: If a premortem is used, sampling a few independent failure lists and keeping causes that recur is the natural extension. The evidence supports pooling answers, not yet failure lists.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Adaptive-Consistency: let's sample step by step
finding: Sampling can stop early once agreement is clear. Agreement among samples is a cheap, model-agnostic signal of item difficulty, and using it cuts cost with almost no accuracy loss.
numbers: 17 reasoning and code datasets, 3 LLMs: sample budget reduced up to 7.9x, average 3.3x, with average accuracy drop under 0.1%. If 9 of the first 10 samples agree, the chance the majority holds after 40 samples is above 99%.
limits: Gates the number of samples, not a premortem step. No test of firing a critique only on low-agreement items.
agent_relevance: Supports a self-consistency gate for G1: fire the failure check when early samples disagree, skip it when they agree (gap 3: mechanism supported, premortem-specific test missing).

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Larger models are well calibrated on multiple choice and true/false. P(True), the model's probability that its own answer is correct, works for self-evaluation and improves when the model first sees many of its own samples. P(IK) calibration is weaker on new tasks.
numbers: Abstract read; no table numbers extracted.
limits: Needs token-probability access. Verbalised confidence after a prompt is a different quantity. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: A cheap trigger candidate: P(True) or sample agreement as a gate for the failure check (gap 3).

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: Distilled written insights from past successes and failures improve an agent with no weight updates. Insights matter most on HotpotQA; stored trajectories matter most on ALFWorld. Combined with Reflexion retries the gains add.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieval-only: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%, ALFWorld 50% vs 55%, WebShop 37% vs 38%. ExpeL matches Reflexion on HotpotQA (40% at round 3 vs 39%). ExpeL plus Reflexion on ALFWorld rises from 59.0% to 64.2% over rounds. Learned insights beat hand-written ones. Adding reflections to insight extraction hurt (hallucinated reflections).
limits: No imagined-failure arm. Small test sets, few seeds.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: stored lessons beat no lessons and stack with retries. Nobody compared them head-to-head with a premortem at equal tokens.

source: Shen, Shen, Yao (2026) CoMem: learning to anticipate failures from retrieved experience
finding: Closest 2026 paper to an LLM premortem on code and math. A small memory module writes failure hypotheses (how this attempt is likely to go wrong) from retrieved past cases, and the solver is guided by them. It beats Reflexion, DoT-Bank and ParamMem. The hypotheses add to test feedback rather than replace it. It requires LoRA fine-tuning of the memory.
numbers: Qwen3-8B, mean of 3 seeds: HumanEval+ Base 81.19, Reflexion 84.87, DoT-Bank 88.14, ParamMem 93.66, CoMem 95.09. LiveCodeBench 41.00, 50.44, 53.89, 56.44, 59.67. MATH 79.38, 86.45, 90.17, 93.76, 94.72. Qwen3-4B HumanEval+ 73.42, 80.37, 85.28, 92.02, 95.30. CoMem over ParamMem (8B): +0.96 MATH, +1.43 HumanEval+, +3.23 LiveCodeBench.
limits: Trained component, so not a prompt-only premortem. Reflexion rows use several attempts with test feedback. There is no arm that prompts a plain 'assume this failed' hypothesis at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Gaps 7 and 8: failure hypotheses grounded in retrieved past cases beat purely self-generated reflection. Supports pairing premortem with an error memory.

source: Kim et al. (2025) InvThink, appendix B.1-B.2 re-read (gaps 1, 5)
finding: Controlled test of direction: failure-enumeration traces and matched positive-goal traces (same 23,063 targets, matched tokens) gave statistically indistinguishable safety after SFT. The default SFT+RL model over-refuses; a calibration term trims this only a little.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-7B SFT: both directions TRIDENT safety 1.000, StrongREJECT attack success 0.000, XSTest false-refusal rate (FRR) 0.980, correct-refusal 1.000. Qwen-3-8B SFT+RL default reward: FRR 0.361, CRR 0.927; with over-refusal term FRR 0.320, CRR 0.920.
limits: Trained models, safety only. Refusal-only SFT data collapsed both arms to a refusal machine, so the null is weak evidence. Not a prompting test.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: no sign that the failure frame itself is the active ingredient. Gap 5: failure enumeration on safety tasks costs helpfulness; measure over-refusal when adding it.

source: Liptay et al. (2026) Bench to the Future 2, text re-read for causal wording (gap 6)
finding: The authors say causal isolation of strategic factors is hard because telling an agent to attend to a factor does not ensure it does. The SOTA forecaster has an imposed rationale structure the single agents lack, so the rank gap may reflect format. No ablation of the pre/post-mortem dimension exists. Expert review covered only 130 of 1,417 questions.
numbers: Top-3 share of Pre/Post-mortem: 37.8% for the SOTA forecaster vs 12.1% and 10.8% (and lower) for single agents. Brier SOTA 0.119 vs Opus 4.6 0.130 (N = 1,367 scored). Cost $1.68 vs $0.55 per question.
limits: Dimension ranking done by Gemini 3.1 Pro, which the authors call subjective. Pre/post-mortem covers both prospective and retrospective reasons. Correlational.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open: the dimension is confounded with rationale format and a 3x cost. Do not cite as causal evidence.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Devil's Advocate: anticipatory reflection, re-read for ablations (gaps 1, 4)
finding: The full text has no ablation isolating the anticipatory step from the post-action check and episode-level plan revision. It reports one bundled method with a 3.5 point gain over the best zero-shot baseline.
numbers: WebArena after 7 episodes: 23.5% vs LATS 22.7% vs Plan+Act 19.8%; plan revisions about 45% fewer than LATS.
limits: Bundled components. Gain over LATS is 0.8 points.
agent_relevance: The anticipation step cannot be credited alone; gap 1 cannot be closed from this paper.

source: Veinott, Klein, Wiggins (2010) re-open attempt via Klein's blog (gap 2)
finding: Could not obtain the ISCRAM paper: the ISCRAM legacy URL gave 404, ResearchGate 403, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited, and the web search budget was spent. Klein's blog gives only N = 178 college students, a hypothetical epidemic scenario, and that premortem students showed the greatest reduction in overconfidence versus critique-only and pros-and-cons groups. No means, SDs, effect sizes or plan-quality measure.
quote: The students in the pre-mortem condition showed the greatest reduction in (over)confidence
limits: Gap 2 stays open. The two earlier secondhand figures (about 25 points; about twice the drop) remain unreconciled. Whatever the means, the outcome is confidence, not plan quality.
agent_relevance: Treat the human evidence as 'premortem lowers confidence', never as 'premortem raises plan quality'.

source: arXiv searches for premortem and related terms via arxiv.org search pages (gap 8)
finding: All-field search 'premortem' gives six hits: InvThink, a prompt-engineering tutorial, uniqueness bias, and three unrelated items. 'pre-mortem' gives BTF-2 plus unrelated items. 'prospective hindsight' gives the RL paper 2610.02740. No paper prompts a literal premortem on planning or coding tasks and reports accuracy against a no-premortem control. Nearest anticipation work: Devil's Advocate (2405.16334), CoMem (2610.25790), and failure-anticipation papers in robotics and vision.
numbers: Six hits for 'premortem'; one relevant hit for 'prospective hindsight'. Crossref and Europe PMC searches added only AUGUR (already b17) and unrelated items.
limits: Search indexes miss papers that use other words (red-teaming own plan, anticipatory, risk-first). Not exhaustive; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 is mostly closed as 'none found': the human premortem has no direct LLM test; trained or bundled variants are the nearest.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: iterative refinement with self-feedback
finding: Self-generated feedback then revision improved GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 outputs on 7 tasks, about 20% absolute on average (abstract). Gains are on tasks where defects are easy to recognise (style, optimisation, dialogue). Later work (Huang, Kamoi) shows reasoning-task gains do not survive a fair comparison.
numbers: Abstract: about 20% absolute average task improvement; up to 13% for strong code models; code optimisation +8.7 over base GPT-4.
limits: Preference-scored and judge-scored tasks; no ground-truth gate. Abstract and a few passages read only.
agent_relevance: Shows the internal-critique positive case: tasks where the critic can recognise defects. Gate on task type (gap 3).

source: Hill (2012) subadditivity, applied to LLM failure listing (gap 5; inference from a12, no new data)
finding: No LLM study measures whether listing failure causes inflates the agent's stated failure probability. The human result (78% subadditive; summed parts 1.07 vs whole 0.82 in the focal group) is the only quantitative base, taken from earlier file a12. InvThink's FRR 0.361 is a related cost on safety tasks only.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 open for calibration: ask for the failure probability before and after the list and compare Brier. Normalising the listed causes might remove the overshoot.

source: Peabody (2017) complexity moderator, used as a gate (gap 3; inference from b06/b25, no new data)
finding: The only direct moderator evidence: premortem added reasons on a complex unfamiliar plan (N = 82) and not on a simple one (N = 72). No study gates a premortem by a computed signal.
agent_relevance: A complexity gate has human-evidence backing; a sample-disagreement gate has LLM-evidence backing (d06). Combine as the G1 trigger.
